div.head: II Atr 2.1
div.ab: ⁊ ðeh hit gedriuen beo ⁊ hit ætfleo to hwilcre friðbyrig, ⁊ ða menn up ætberstan into ðære byrig, ðonne habban ða men frið ⁊ þæt hy him mid bringað.
Et licet abacta sit et applicetur ad aliquam curiam pacis, et homines euadant in ipsam curiam, pacem habeant et quod attulerint secum.
⁊ ðeh hit gedriuen beo ⁊ hit ætfleo to hwilcre friðbyrig, ⁊ ða menn up ætberstan into ðære byrig, ðonne habban ða men frið ⁊ þæt hy him mid bringað.

Und selbst wenn es [nur] angetrieben worden ist und es flüchtet zu irgend einer Stadt jenes Friedensgebietes, und die [Schiffs]leute gelangen an Land in die Stadt, so sollen die Leute und was sie mit sich bringen Friedensschutz erhalten.

And even if it has been driven ashore and takes refuge at any town of that peace-area, and the [ship's] men escape onto land into the town, then let the men and what they bring with them have protection.
And even if it is pursued and reach any town included in the truce and the men escape into the town, protection is to be afforded to them and to what they bring with them.
And even if it is driven ashore, and takes refuge in any borough included in the truce, and the men escape into the borough, the men and what they bring with them are to have peace.

note.seg: ‘Asyl, jedoch nicht im sonst gewohnten Sinne innerer Heiligkeit, sondern staatlichen Privilegs für bestimmte Häfen’; Kemble Saxons II 95. Diese Bed. ist fürs Nordische im 10./11. Jh. bezeugt: Nach Irland verschlagene Isländer versehen sich feindlicher Behandlung, ‘denn wir sind fern von Häfen oder Kaufstätten, wo Ausländer Frieden haben’; und Guthormr, Olafs d. Heil. Neffe, hatte in Dublin friðland; Mogk Kelten im 9. Jh. 21. 23.—Bei Angelsachsen ist dieser Sondersinn für frið- burg oder die Einrichtung bestimmter Asylhäfen, in denen kein Strandrecht walte, unbekannt. [Nur entfernt ähnliche Bed. hat friðstow und beansprucht später London; s. d. Gl 52; Asyl 3. 17c.] Ich verstehe also ‘befestigten Englischen Hafen [mit Markt]’; denn der andere Kontrahent, das Heer, besass ein Landgebiet, wenigstens vom Standpunkte Englischen Staatsrechts, nicht, oder höchstens faktisch und vorübergehend

‘Asylum, though not in the otherwise usual sense of inner sanctity, but in that of a state privilege for particular harbours’; Kemble Saxons II 95. This meaning is attested in the Norse world in the 10th/11th cent.: Icelanders driven off course to Ireland expect hostile treatment, ‘for we are far from harbours or trading places where foreigners have peace’; and Guthormr, nephew of Olaf the Saint, had friðland in Dublin; Mogk Kelten im 9. Jh. 21. 23.—Among the Anglo-Saxons this special sense of frið- burg, or the institution of particular harbours of refuge in which no right of wreck prevailed, is unknown. [friðstow has only a remotely similar meaning, and London later lays claim to it; see that word in Gl 52; Asyl 3. 17c.] I therefore understand ‘fortified English harbour [with a market]’; for the other contracting party, the army, possessed no territory, at least from the standpoint of English public law, or at most de facto and temporarily

Cf. friðman, 3; 3, 1 and 4. In the north during the tenth and eleventh centuries certain places enjoyed special protection as trading centres, so that merchants from far and wide could bring their goods there without fear of molestation (see Du Chaillu, Viking Age, ii. p. 210, and cf. Laxdael Saga, Ch. 21, where it is said of Ireland: þetta er fiarri höfnum ok þeim kaupstöðum, er útlendir menn skulu hafa frið). Such appointment of special havens of refuge, as Liebermann points out, was unknown in England, so that frið is to be taken here in the same sense as elsewhere in the treaty.
